05a17237-cf8b-4c14-a8b7-e57886877cf3.name: PHP2Shell - PHP Core Remote Code Execution

threat.description:
Pre-authentication remote code execution in the PHP core interpreter, tracked as
CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and named PHP2Shell by the discovering
researchers at Calif. Each is rated CVSS v4.0 9.2. Patched releases shipped
2026-10-21 after an embargo break forced the date forward. Exploitation is
confirmed, broad, and predates disclosure.

ROOT CAUSE (confirmed by the discoverers, no longer speculative)

The bug class is interrupted cleanup. PHP leaves dangling pointers and stale
interpreter state when an allocation would exceed memory_limit, or when another
fatal error interrupts native code before its normal cleanup completes. Request
shutdown then frees memory that surviving state still references. Calif found
two general OOM fatal producers and three distinct interruptible points. The
earliest affected path dates to PHP 5.4.0, and the paths are exploitable under
default configuration.

HOW THE ATTACKER FORCES THE FATAL

Two request-shaping tricks, both of which leave structural traces a proxy can
see:

  1. post_max_size bypass. PHP compares post_max_size against the declared
     Content-Length before automatic POST parsing, but does not enforce the same
     limit against the bytes it actually consumes. A chunked HTTP/1.1 or a
     lengthless HTTP/2 multipart request therefore passes the check with no
     meaningful declared length. A configured input-decompression filter creates
     the same mismatch between compressed and decoded length.
  2. Memory exhaustion while staying under post_max_size. An RFC1867 upload part
     with filename="" carries no file data and is not counted toward
     max_file_uploads, yet PHP still creates all six $_FILES entries (name,
     full_path, type, tmp_name, error, size). When the field name is nested, for
     example files[a][b][c], PHP builds that hierarchy separately for each of the
     six entries, so one short empty-upload record expands into many native
     HashTables, Buckets and string-key allocations. Hundreds of such records
     exceed the default 128 MiB heap while the whole body stays under the default
     8 MiB post_max_size.

THREE EXPLOITATION PATHS, AND WHY THE SAPI DECIDES EVERYTHING

This is the most operationally important part of the writeup, because it inverts
the usual assumption that PHP-FPM is the main surface.

  Path 1, Apache mod_php, PHP >= 7.3, arbitrary PHP scripts.
    _zend_hash_str_add_or_update_i increments both nNumUsed and nNumOfElements
    before the bucket is initialised, so the bucket becomes teardown-visible
    before its key allocation. A fatal in that allocation skips the key, hash and
    zval assignments while the count stays incremented, and teardown later
    consumes stale bytes as a live bucket. Reached through ordinary request
    variable registration during php_request_startup(), before the target script
    runs.

  Path 2, Apache mod_php, PHP >= 5.4.0, arbitrary PHP scripts.
    Session upload-progress opens and updates a session while the request body is
    still being parsed, before PHP considers its modules activated. If parsing
    fatals, the multipart END callback is skipped and request shutdown gates
    extension shutdown on the activation flag, so session RSHUTDOWN never runs.
    The heap is freed anyway and the Apache worker survives with PS(id) and
    PS(http_session_vars) dangling. A second multipart request carrying a session
    ID and the PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS field but NO file part reaches
    MULTIPART_EVENT_END without passing FILE_START, so the early session reset
    never happens and cleanup operates on freed state.

  Path 3, Apache mod_php and PHP-FPM, application-dependent.
    PHP's generic unserializer publishes shared bookkeeping in the Basic
    extension's globals. A fatal inside a live decode skips
    php_var_unserialize_destroy(), leaving BG(unserialize).data dangling with a
    nonzero nesting level. Because this fatal lands after successful request
    startup, PHP-FPM keeps the worker. The next multipart request reaches session
    upload-progress before Basic's RINIT and the stale nesting level makes the
    dangling pointer look like an active nested decoder. Requires the application
    to expose a reachable post-startup decode: session_start(), session_decode(),
    unserialize(), or a wrapper such as WordPress's maybe_unserialize().

  The asymmetry: on mod_php, PHP runs inside the Apache worker and request
  shutdown executes even after startup failure, so the malformed state is
  consumed and the worker is reused. On PHP-FPM, a startup failure takes the
  process-exit branch (FPM_EXIT_SOFTWARE) and the worker dies before anything
  can consume the state, which is why paths 1 and 2 do not apply to it. mod_php
  is therefore the critical surface: universally exploitable against arbitrary
  scripts. PHP-FPM is exploitable only through path 3 and only where the
  application decodes attacker-influenced or memory-pressure-adjacent data.

CONFIRMED PRE-AUTH RCE TARGETS

Calif confirmed pre-authentication RCE against WordPress 7.1.2, Drupal 11.4.3,
Joomla 6.1.4, MediaWiki 1.46.2, Roundcube 1.7.4, Magento 2.4.9, phpMyAdmin 5.2.3,
Nextcloud 35.0.1, Laravel 13.11, Symfony 8.1 and WHMCS, plus arbitrary PHP
scripts in some instances. This is not a niche configuration issue.

EXPLOITATION IN THE WILD, EARLIER THAN DISCLOSURE

Amazon Threat Intelligence found a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt in MadPot
honeypot telemetry dated 2026-10-17, four days before disclosure, from an IP
associated with a commercial anonymisation network. Further attempts followed
between 02:00 and 08:00 UTC on 2026-10-21, before the 14:00 UTC embargo lift,
with varied payloads and anonymisation infrastructure suggesting multiple
distinct actors. More proof-of-concept code appeared within hours of the release
and was used against AWS sensors almost immediately. It is now broadly exploited.

Investigations should start from 2026-10-17 at the latest, not from the
disclosure date. Coordinated disclosure ran from 2026-08-11 and a researcher
published a hash of one finding on 2026-08-05, so an earlier bound cannot be
excluded, though no exploitation has been reported before 2026-10-17.

LINEAGE: EXPECT SIBLINGS

The class has a twenty-year history. Stefan Esser found the first PHP memory
limit remote vulnerability in 2004; bug #78876 (multipart/form-data causing OOM)
was reported in 2020 and incidentally shielded HHVM; OSTIF and Quarkslab
identified a related issue in a 2024 audit without proving exploitation. Calif
generalised its first finding into a reusable pattern (publish or destroy state,
then perform fallible work, then initialise or commit, where a nonlocal fatal
during the fallible work skips the commit and a surviving consumer trusts false
state) and that pattern immediately produced the second finding. Two consequences
for detection: more siblings are likely in PHP and in comparable interpreters, and
CVE-specific signatures will age badly. Detection content for this threat should
key on the mechanism and on post-exploitation behaviour, not on these two CVE
identifiers.

MITIGATION REALITY

Patching is the only complete remediation. Both AWS and Calif state plainly that
no configuration-only workaround fully addresses both issues. Calif's temporary,
partial mitigations are not what the early reporting suggested, and differ by
SAPI:

  - mod_php: set memory_limit=-1.
  - PHP-FPM: set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and memory_limit=-1.

memory_limit is the common factor, because removing the cap removes the fatal the
exploit depends on. That trade is not free: memory_limit=-1 removes PHP's memory
cap and raises the risk of host memory exhaustion, so it is a deliberate
availability trade, not a safe default. Disabling session upload-progress alone
closes only one path and does nothing for mod_php. AWS additionally suggests
blocking multipart file uploads where patching is blocked, after assessing
application impact, and publishes an AWS WAF mitigation guide.

Content in this description was rephrased from the sources in the references for
compliance with licensing restrictions.
threat.terrain:
Ranked by exploitability, not by population.

Critical: Apache with mod_php on PHP 5.4.0 or later, internet-facing. Paths 1 and
2 give RCE against arbitrary PHP scripts under default configuration, with no
application precondition and no authentication.

High: PHP-FPM and php-cgi behind Apache HTTP or NGINX, where the application
performs a reachable post-startup decode (session_start, session_decode,
unserialize, or wrappers such as WordPress's maybe_unserialize). Path 3 only, so
exploitability is application-dependent, but the qualifying call is present in
most real CMS and framework stacks.

The affected application population covers CMS and e-commerce (WordPress,
WooCommerce, Drupal, Joomla, Magento and Adobe Commerce), collaboration and
webmail (MediaWiki, Nextcloud, Roundcube), administration interfaces
(phpMyAdmin, WHMCS) and framework-based bespoke applications (Laravel, Symfony).

Secondary: CI runners executing PHP build and test code, and container images
pinning a PHP base layer, where a rebuild rather than a package update is needed.
Shared and managed hosting concentrates the unpatchable population and sits
outside direct control.

Inventory note: record the version and SAPI that actually serves web requests.
The CLI binary and the web SAPI can differ on the same host, and the SAPI
determines which of the three paths apply.

bdc58fee-8da6-4fc9-8fbd-30f8fd156bc7.name: Powershell with encoded payload passed to cmdline

threat.terrain:
A threat actors need an initial access to the system to use PowerShell
console to execute commands to obfuscate their traffic and activities.
threat.description:
When working with PowerShell, a threat actor can encode a command or script
using Base64 or other type of encoding and pass it as a parameter to the
command line. This technique is useful for obfuscating sensitive
information or executing complex commands. (ref [1])   


The malicious document contains a macro which, upon execution,
creates a batch script at C:\Users\public\new[.]bat with the
following content:  

powershell -exec bypass -noP -w hidden -nonI -enc"{string}" del %0;

Other possible examples for encoding with PowerShell commands: 

Encoding a Command with Base64

1. Create a command as a string. 

$command = 'dir "C:\Program Files"'

2. Convert the command to Base64:

$bytes = [System.Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetBytes($command)
$encodedCommand = [Convert]::ToBase64String($bytes)

Now you can run the encoded command using powershell.exe:

powershell.exe -encodedCommand $encodedCommand

It's also possible to encode domain names, for example: 

Powershell input:

[Convert]::ToBase64String([System.Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetBytes("'sample_domain.com'"))

Threat actors also use PowerShell scripts for faster encoding process and result.  

An example of Powershell script (ref [2])  

param(
[Parameter()][Alias("un")][string]$Username,
[Parameter()][Alias("pw")][string]$Password
)

Write-Host "Username: $Username"
Write-Host "Password: $Password"

3c0b7355-2f44-4632-89a9-a9cdb4fa9de9.name: PHP2Shell Exploitation and Post-Exploitation on the Web Application Tier

objective.description:
Detect exploitation of the PHP core remote code execution flaws CVE-2026-109618
and CVE-2026-109619 (PHP2Shell) at both the attempt stage and the
post-exploitation stage.

Version 1 of this objective covered post-exploitation only, on the reasoning that
no trigger signature was possible. That reasoning is now obsolete. Calif has
published the root cause, and the mechanism turns out to have structural features
an attacker cannot easily vary: the exploit must first force a PHP fatal by
exceeding memory_limit, and the cheapest way to do that is a multipart body
stuffed with empty-filename upload parts carrying deeply nested bracket field
names, delivered chunked or over HTTP/2 so the declared length never trips
post_max_size. Two of the three paths then require a follow-up multipart request
carrying PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS with no file part. Those are request
properties, not payload bytes, so they survive payload obfuscation.

The objective therefore has two halves. Signals 4 and 5 cover the attempt: a
server-side view (memory_limit fatals and PHP-FPM worker exits) and a
request-side view (multipart shaped for heap exhaustion). Both can fire before
the attacker achieves anything, which matters because AWS observed exploitation
from 2026-10-17, four days before disclosure. Signals 1 to 3 cover what the
attacker does with code execution once they have it, and they are what makes this
objective durable: Calif generalised the bug into a reusable pattern and expects
siblings, so CVE-specific coverage will age while behavioural coverage will not.
AWS reaches the same conclusion independently and advises investing in detections
that do not depend on a per-CVE signature.

SAPI ASYMMETRY DRIVES COVERAGE, AND IT IS COUNTERINTUITIVE

On Apache mod_php, PHP runs inside the Apache worker, request shutdown runs even
after a startup failure, and the worker is reused. Exploitation succeeds against
arbitrary PHP scripts, and the post-exploitation signals fire with apache2 or
httpd as the parent process, never a php binary. On PHP-FPM, a startup failure
exits the worker before anything can consume the malformed state, so two of the
three paths simply do not work, and an attempt shows up as a worker exit rather
than as code execution. The practical consequence: signals 1 to 3 carry mod_php
coverage, signal 4 carries PHP-FPM attempt coverage, and only the
application-dependent third path produces execution on PHP-FPM. A detection
estate that watched only php-fpm process ancestry would have had the asymmetry
exactly backwards.

Scope boundary: this objective covers exploitation and post-exploitation on the
PHP application tier. It does not cover interpreter inventory or version exposure,
which is vulnerability-management work, nor the partial configuration mitigations
(memory_limit=-1 on mod_php, plus session.upload_progress.enabled=0 on PHP-FPM),
neither of which replaces a patch. It also does not include matching on the
anonymisation-network addresses AWS published: AWS states they are shared
infrastructure to investigate on observation rather than block, so they belong in
rule triage procedures, not in a detection.

signals.name: PHP SAPI worker spawns an OS command interpreter or network client
signals.description:
A process whose parent is a PHP interpreter or web server worker (php-fpm,
php-cgi, php, httpd, apache2, nginx) executes a shell, scripting
interpreter, download client, or network utility. This is the highest
fidelity observable for the objective: a healthy PHP application tier
rarely shells out, and when it does the set of legitimate callers is small
and enumerable per environment.

The apache2 and httpd parents are not padding. Under mod_php the
interpreter is embedded in the Apache worker, so successful exploitation of
the two universally exploitable paths produces a child of apache2 or httpd
with no php process anywhere in the ancestry. mod_php is the critical
surface here, which makes those two parent names the most important entries
in the list rather than an afterthought.

True positive proves arbitrary code execution under the web service
account, independent of which vulnerability or application flaw delivered
it. Known benign callers: deployment and cache-warm hooks, ImageMagick and
ffmpeg wrappers, mail transport helpers, and composer running in a
container entrypoint. These are environment-specific and must be enumerated
into the rule exclusion block rather than removed from the signal.

data.availability: Linux endpoint process telemetry on the web application tier
data.requirements:
Process-creation events with both the child image and the parent image.
Sysmon for Linux (event ID 1), Falco, Tetragon, or an EDR agent satisfy
this. Plain auditd EXECVE records do not: they carry a numeric ppid but
no parent image, so the parent must be resolved by correlation, which
degrades precision. Declare the agent coverage gap for any web host that
has none.

signals.name: Web-served file written by the PHP runtime
signals.description:
A PHP SAPI worker, or an Apache worker running mod_php, creates or modifies a
file under a web-served directory, most significantly a single-file PHP
script with obfuscated content. This is the persistence half of the attack: a
web shell in a writable web root survives the interpreter patch and gives the
attacker a stable channel that no longer depends on the vulnerability. It
also survives the mitigation path, since memory_limit=-1 removes the fatal
the exploit needs but does nothing about access already established.

Precision depends entirely on how the application manages its own writable
paths. Upload directories, template and asset caches, and session storage
are legitimately written by PHP all day. The signal is only usable once
those paths are enumerated and excluded, and it is strongest when scoped to
files that the web server will interpret as code.

data.availability: Linux endpoint file telemetry on the web application tier
data.requirements:
File-create and file-modify events with the writing process image and the
target path. Sysmon for Linux (event ID 11), Falco, Tetragon, or EDR
file telemetry satisfy this. Requires a maintained inventory of web-root
paths and application-writable subdirectories per service to be tunable.

signals.name: First-seen egress from a web tier host after an inbound request burst
signals.description:
A host in the web application tier opens an outbound connection to a
destination not seen in its own historical baseline, shortly after a burst
of inbound requests. Covers the command-and-control and tool-transfer step
for cases where the execution and file signals are blind, for example a
memory-only payload on a host without process telemetry.

Lower precision by construction. Web tier hosts legitimately reach package
mirrors, API partners, certificate authorities, telemetry endpoints and
object storage, and new destinations appear whenever a dependency or a
partner changes. Treat as a correlation contributor rather than a
standalone alert unless the baseline is narrow and well maintained.

data.availability: Network or proxy egress logs scoped to the web application tier
data.requirements:
Outbound connection records with source host, destination address and
port, from firewall, proxy, or endpoint network telemetry. Needs at least
14 days of per-host destination history to build a baseline, and an
asset-tag or subnet definition that identifies the web tier.

signals.name: PHP memory_limit exhaustion fatals and PHP-FPM worker exits during request parsing
signals.description:
A rise in PHP fatal errors reporting that the allowed memory size was
exhausted, and in PHP-FPM worker exits or pool restarts, coinciding with
elevated multipart POST volume on the same host. This is the server-side view
of the attempt stage, and the single cheapest signal in the objective: it
needs only logs PHP already writes.

Version 1 of this signal looked for worker segfaults on the assumption of
heap use-after-free crashes. The published root cause corrects that. The
exploit deliberately drives an allocation past memory_limit to produce a
controlled fatal, so the primary artefact is an out-of-memory fatal during
request startup or multipart parsing, not a segmentation fault. On PHP-FPM
the two startup-stage paths take the process-exit branch, so an attempt
presents as a clean worker exit, which is why worker exits belong in this
signal alongside the fatals.

Severity is Medium rather than High because the signal detects the
precondition, not the compromise, and because it is noisy on its own:
genuine application memory bugs, undersized memory_limit, large legitimate
uploads and extension incompatibilities after an upgrade all produce the same
fatal. It needs a per-host baseline and becomes meaningful when the fatal rate
departs from it while multipart POST volume rises. Two caveats worth holding:
a patched interpreter does not silence it, since scanning patched hosts still
produces fatals, and a host mitigated with memory_limit=-1 goes silent on this
signal entirely because the cap that produces the fatal has been removed.

data.availability: PHP error logs, PHP-FPM pool logs, and web access logs
data.requirements:
PHP error log or syslog carrying fatal error text including the allowed
memory size exhaustion message, plus PHP-FPM pool logs recording worker
exits and restarts, correlated with web access logs exposing request method
and content type. Requires PHP-FPM log level at notice or above so worker
exits are recorded, log_errors enabled with a reachable error_log
destination, and a per-host fatal-rate baseline over at least 7 days.

signals.name: Multipart request shaped to exhaust the PHP heap or to consume stale session state
signals.description:
The request-side view of the attempt stage, covering two distinct shapes that
together span all three exploitation paths.

Shape A, forcing the fatal. A multipart/form-data POST carrying many upload
parts with an empty filename (filename="") and deeply nested bracket field
names such as files[a][b][c], typically delivered with chunked
transfer-encoding or over HTTP/2 so no meaningful Content-Length is declared.
Each of those empty parts is uncounted against max_file_uploads yet still
expands into six nested $_FILES hierarchies, so a body well under the 8 MiB
default post_max_size can exhaust the 128 MiB default heap. The giveaway is
the ratio: a high part count and deep field nesting against a small body.

Shape B, consuming the stale state. A multipart/form-data POST carrying a
session ID and the PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS field but containing no file
part at all. This is the follow-up request for the session upload-progress
path: with no file part it reaches the multipart END handler without ever
passing FILE_START, so the early session reset is skipped and cleanup runs
against freed state.

Shape B is the precise form of the broader guidance AWS published. AWS
advises looking for POST requests containing the PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS
string; that field appears in legitimate upload-progress use, so the string
alone is noisy. The same field with no accompanying file part has no
legitimate purpose and is markedly more specific.

Recall caveats. The field name is the value of the server's
session.upload_progress.name setting and only defaults to
PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS, so a customised deployment expects a different
string. Shape A tolerates variation in part count, nesting depth and encoding,
so thresholds must be set on the shape rather than on exact values. Neither
shape evidences success, only an attempt consistent with the published
mechanism.

data.availability: WAF or reverse-proxy logs with request body inspection
data.requirements:
Request body visibility. This is the binding constraint and it is not
satisfied by ordinary web access logs: combined-format access logs record
the request line and headers, never the multipart body, so neither shape is
visible in them. Requires a WAF, reverse proxy or mod_security-style audit
log that captures or evaluates POST bodies, plus retention of
Transfer-Encoding and HTTP protocol version to identify the lengthless
delivery. Where only header-level telemetry exists, the achievable
approximation is multipart POST volume per source against endpoints that
accept no uploads, which is a much weaker signal and should be documented
as a gap rather than presented as coverage.

composition.description:
Each signal stands alone. The execution and file-write signals are
high-fidelity enough to alert on their own, and holding them for
corroboration would trade away the only short window in which a web shell can
be caught before it is used. The attempt-stage signals are kept independent so
that an organisation whose process telemetry is incomplete still sees something,
and so that the request-shape signal can alert on a WAF even where no endpoint
agent exists at all, which is exactly the shared-hosting and legacy-branch
population most exposed here.

Sequence composition is genuinely tempting now that the mechanism is public,
because two of the three paths require an ordered pair of requests: one that
fatals and leaves state dangling, then a later multipart request that consumes
it in the surviving worker. It is still the wrong choice for the alerting path.
The first path needs no second request, the pair can arrive minutes or hours
apart through different anonymisation egress points, and AWS observed varied
payloads from multiple actors, so a rigid ordering assumption would create a
bypass. The A-then-B pairing belongs in rule triage, where it raises confidence,
rather than in composition, where it would gate alerting.

Threshold composition was also rejected: successful exploitation generates one
execution event, not several.

objective.investment:
Moderate, now weighted towards the request-side signal. The execution and
file-write signals reuse Linux process and file telemetry already required for
other Linux detections, so their cost is tuning rather than onboarding, and the
memory_limit fatal signal needs only logs PHP already writes.

Three prerequisites carry real effort. An inventory of web-root and
application-writable paths per service, needed before the file-write signal is
tunable. Closing the process-telemetry gap on web hosts that run no agent.
Request body inspection at the WAF or reverse proxy, which the request-shape
signal depends on absolutely and which no amount of access-log work substitutes
for.

One inventory item is worth the effort on its own: which hosts run mod_php rather
than PHP-FPM. The SAPI determines which exploitation paths apply and therefore
which signals can fire, so it changes both triage priority and expected coverage.

bfeb24bf-8a17-4ccc-8aec-91721743153d.name: Powershell encoded payload to start new process

objective.description:
Detect and alert on powershell encoded payload to start new process activity.

This detection objective was migrated from a Cyber Detection Model (CDM).

composition.description: Each signal triggers independently, covering different detection approaches for the same objective.

signals.name: Powershell encoded payload to start new process
signals.description:
Adversaries use PowerShell to execute local scripts and execute remote resources
after retrieving them using multiple network protocols. They can also encode payloads
using the command line and load PowerShell into other processes.

Here are some examples of encoded PowerShell payloads and how they can be detected:

### Base64-Encoded Payload

#### background

A common technique is to encode the entire PowerShell script in Base64 and execute it using
the -encodedcommand switch.

To detect this, look for:
- Execution of powershell.exe with encode arguments
- The presence of base64 string in the command line

#### detection strategies

to detect base64encoded string, you may use REGEX and then you may have the
option on the detection platform to decode the base64 encoded string to
confirm the actions done.

When focusing on specific keywords within the encoded string, a very good
approach is to precompute the base64 encoded version of the keyword and
search for that pattern in strings. To precompute the base64 string, 3
scenario have to be considered:
- the keyword is at a boundary of a 3-character block
- the keyword starts at second character of a 3-character block
- the keyword starts at the third character of 3-character block

Malicious payloads are often encoded and obfuscated, with PowerShell commands frequently
used to download them from the internet. To detect encoded and downloadable command line
arguments, it is essential to examine PowerShell logs, such as Sysmon or Windows PowerShell logs,
for the presence of specific keywords like "Net.WebClient," "DownloadFile," "Invoke-WebRequest,"
"Invoke-Shellcode," "http:," "-enc," "-encodedCommand," "-e," "-ec," "-en," "-encod," and "-enco".

Additionally, you can visit the following page to access a PowerShell Watchlist that helps with detection. [4]

For example, this CDM attemtps to detect the launch of a process
using the cmdlet "Start-Process". Preprocessing this keyword gives
the following search strings (without decoding base64 nor REGEX)

| Keyword | offset | string (with leading _ or *) | search string |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Start-Process | 0 | U3RhcnQtUHJvY2Vzcw== | U3RhcnQtUHJvY2Vz |
| Start-Process | 1 | X1N0YXJ0LVByb2Nlc3M= / KlN0YXJ0LVByb2Nlc3M= | N0YXJ0LVByb2Nl |
| Start-Process | 2 | X19TdGFydC1Qcm9jZXNz / KipTdGFydC1Qcm9jZXNz | TdGFydC1Qcm9jZXNz |

### Obfuscated Payload with Special Characters

Adversaries may also obfuscate the PowerShell script using special characters.

To detect this, look for:
- Execution of powershell.exe with the -nop, -w hidden, and -c arguments
- High counts of obfuscation characters like `, `, and '

Useful telemetry will include:

- Windows Security Event ID 400: PowerShell command-line logging
- Windows Security Event IDs 800 and 4103: Module loading and Add-Type logging
- Windows Security Event ID 4688 : A new process has been created including process command-line
- Sysmon Event IDs 1 and 7: Process creation and Image loaded

Tuning considerations:
- Monitor for any attempts to enable scripts running on a system would be considered suspicious.
If scripts are not commonly used on a system, but enabled, scripts running out of cycle from patching
or other administrator functions are suspicious. Scripts should be captured from the file system when
possible to determine their actions and intent.
- Monitor for newly executed processes that may abuse PowerShell commands and scripts for execution.
PowerShell is a scripting environment included with Windows that is used by both attackers and administrators.
Execution of PowerShell scripts in most Windows versions is opaque and not typically secured by antivirus
which makes using PowerShell an easy way to circumvent security measures.
- Encoded PowerShell can be abused to avoid any complexity with special characters that can be difficult
to handle.

data.requirements:
Data collection: Carbon Black EDR Connectors, Sysmon Logs, Windows Security Logs.
Data sources: Command, File, Script, Module, Process.

data.availability: Linux endpoint process telemetry on the web application tier
data.requirements:
Process-creation events with both the child image and the parent image.
Sysmon for Linux (event ID 1), Falco, Tetragon, or an EDR agent satisfy
this. Plain auditd EXECVE records do not: they carry a numeric ppid but
no parent image, so the parent must be resolved by correlation, which
degrades precision. Declare the agent coverage gap for any web host that
has none.

5c99727b-3ed8-4538-9757-866f417c22a6.name: Web-served file written by the PHP runtime
5c99727b-3ed8-4538-9757-866f417c22a6.description:
A PHP SAPI worker, or an Apache worker running mod_php, creates or modifies a
file under a web-served directory, most significantly a single-file PHP
script with obfuscated content. This is the persistence half of the attack: a
web shell in a writable web root survives the interpreter patch and gives the
attacker a stable channel that no longer depends on the vulnerability. It
also survives the mitigation path, since memory_limit=-1 removes the fatal
the exploit needs but does nothing about access already established.

Precision depends entirely on how the application manages its own writable
paths. Upload directories, template and asset caches, and session storage
are legitimately written by PHP all day. The signal is only usable once
those paths are enumerated and excluded, and it is strongest when scoped to
files that the web server will interpret as code.

data.availability: Linux endpoint file telemetry on the web application tier
data.requirements:
File-create and file-modify events with the writing process image and the
target path. Sysmon for Linux (event ID 11), Falco, Tetragon, or EDR
file telemetry satisfy this. Requires a maintained inventory of web-root
paths and application-writable subdirectories per service to be tunable.

d7437c01-261e-4aa0-aa8e-4fa7ac6ebde2.name: First-seen egress from a web tier host after an inbound request burst
d7437c01-261e-4aa0-aa8e-4fa7ac6ebde2.description:
A host in the web application tier opens an outbound connection to a
destination not seen in its own historical baseline, shortly after a burst
of inbound requests. Covers the command-and-control and tool-transfer step
for cases where the execution and file signals are blind, for example a
memory-only payload on a host without process telemetry.

Lower precision by construction. Web tier hosts legitimately reach package
mirrors, API partners, certificate authorities, telemetry endpoints and
object storage, and new destinations appear whenever a dependency or a
partner changes. Treat as a correlation contributor rather than a
standalone alert unless the baseline is narrow and well maintained.

data.availability: Network or proxy egress logs scoped to the web application tier
data.requirements:
Outbound connection records with source host, destination address and
port, from firewall, proxy, or endpoint network telemetry. Needs at least
14 days of per-host destination history to build a baseline, and an
asset-tag or subnet definition that identifies the web tier.

1b25e502-c486-423b-8c19-a1d458e70a87.name: PHP memory_limit exhaustion fatals and PHP-FPM worker exits during request parsing
1b25e502-c486-423b-8c19-a1d458e70a87.description:
A rise in PHP fatal errors reporting that the allowed memory size was
exhausted, and in PHP-FPM worker exits or pool restarts, coinciding with
elevated multipart POST volume on the same host. This is the server-side view
of the attempt stage, and the single cheapest signal in the objective: it
needs only logs PHP already writes.

Version 1 of this signal looked for worker segfaults on the assumption of
heap use-after-free crashes. The published root cause corrects that. The
exploit deliberately drives an allocation past memory_limit to produce a
controlled fatal, so the primary artefact is an out-of-memory fatal during
request startup or multipart parsing, not a segmentation fault. On PHP-FPM
the two startup-stage paths take the process-exit branch, so an attempt
presents as a clean worker exit, which is why worker exits belong in this
signal alongside the fatals.

Severity is Medium rather than High because the signal detects the
precondition, not the compromise, and because it is noisy on its own:
genuine application memory bugs, undersized memory_limit, large legitimate
uploads and extension incompatibilities after an upgrade all produce the same
fatal. It needs a per-host baseline and becomes meaningful when the fatal rate
departs from it while multipart POST volume rises. Two caveats worth holding:
a patched interpreter does not silence it, since scanning patched hosts still
produces fatals, and a host mitigated with memory_limit=-1 goes silent on this
signal entirely because the cap that produces the fatal has been removed.

data.availability: PHP error logs, PHP-FPM pool logs, and web access logs
data.requirements:
PHP error log or syslog carrying fatal error text including the allowed
memory size exhaustion message, plus PHP-FPM pool logs recording worker
exits and restarts, correlated with web access logs exposing request method
and content type. Requires PHP-FPM log level at notice or above so worker
exits are recorded, log_errors enabled with a reachable error_log
destination, and a per-host fatal-rate baseline over at least 7 days.

6fc0c236-6f80-4ab1-8dd8-1281096079da.name: Multipart request shaped to exhaust the PHP heap or to consume stale session state
6fc0c236-6f80-4ab1-8dd8-1281096079da.description:
The request-side view of the attempt stage, covering two distinct shapes that
together span all three exploitation paths.

Shape A, forcing the fatal. A multipart/form-data POST carrying many upload
parts with an empty filename (filename="") and deeply nested bracket field
names such as files[a][b][c], typically delivered with chunked
transfer-encoding or over HTTP/2 so no meaningful Content-Length is declared.
Each of those empty parts is uncounted against max_file_uploads yet still
expands into six nested $_FILES hierarchies, so a body well under the 8 MiB
default post_max_size can exhaust the 128 MiB default heap. The giveaway is
the ratio: a high part count and deep field nesting against a small body.

Shape B, consuming the stale state. A multipart/form-data POST carrying a
session ID and the PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS field but containing no file
part at all. This is the follow-up request for the session upload-progress
path: with no file part it reaches the multipart END handler without ever
passing FILE_START, so the early session reset is skipped and cleanup runs
against freed state.

Shape B is the precise form of the broader guidance AWS published. AWS
advises looking for POST requests containing the PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS
string; that field appears in legitimate upload-progress use, so the string
alone is noisy. The same field with no accompanying file part has no
legitimate purpose and is markedly more specific.

Recall caveats. The field name is the value of the server's
session.upload_progress.name setting and only defaults to
PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS, so a customised deployment expects a different
string. Shape A tolerates variation in part count, nesting depth and encoding,
so thresholds must be set on the shape rather than on exact values. Neither
shape evidences success, only an attempt consistent with the published
mechanism.

data.availability: WAF or reverse-proxy logs with request body inspection
data.requirements:
Request body visibility. This is the binding constraint and it is not
satisfied by ordinary web access logs: combined-format access logs record
the request line and headers, never the multipart body, so neither shape is
visible in them. Requires a WAF, reverse proxy or mod_security-style audit
log that captures or evaluates POST bodies, plus retention of
Transfer-Encoding and HTTP protocol version to identify the lengthless
delivery. Where only header-level telemetry exists, the achievable
approximation is multipart POST volume per source against endpoints that
accept no uploads, which is a much weaker signal and should be documented
as a gap rather than presented as coverage.

cf9c69a2-9317-4f0f-9506-fbeeb1c73ff0.name: Powershell encoded payload to start new process
cf9c69a2-9317-4f0f-9506-fbeeb1c73ff0.description:
Adversaries use PowerShell to execute local scripts and execute remote resources
after retrieving them using multiple network protocols. They can also encode payloads
using the command line and load PowerShell into other processes.

Here are some examples of encoded PowerShell payloads and how they can be detected:

### Base64-Encoded Payload

#### background

A common technique is to encode the entire PowerShell script in Base64 and execute it using
the -encodedcommand switch.

To detect this, look for:
- Execution of powershell.exe with encode arguments
- The presence of base64 string in the command line

#### detection strategies

to detect base64encoded string, you may use REGEX and then you may have the
option on the detection platform to decode the base64 encoded string to
confirm the actions done.

When focusing on specific keywords within the encoded string, a very good
approach is to precompute the base64 encoded version of the keyword and
search for that pattern in strings. To precompute the base64 string, 3
scenario have to be considered:
- the keyword is at a boundary of a 3-character block
- the keyword starts at second character of a 3-character block
- the keyword starts at the third character of 3-character block

Malicious payloads are often encoded and obfuscated, with PowerShell commands frequently
used to download them from the internet. To detect encoded and downloadable command line
arguments, it is essential to examine PowerShell logs, such as Sysmon or Windows PowerShell logs,
for the presence of specific keywords like "Net.WebClient," "DownloadFile," "Invoke-WebRequest,"
"Invoke-Shellcode," "http:," "-enc," "-encodedCommand," "-e," "-ec," "-en," "-encod," and "-enco".

Additionally, you can visit the following page to access a PowerShell Watchlist that helps with detection. [4]

For example, this CDM attemtps to detect the launch of a process
using the cmdlet "Start-Process". Preprocessing this keyword gives
the following search strings (without decoding base64 nor REGEX)

| Keyword | offset | string (with leading _ or *) | search string |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Start-Process | 0 | U3RhcnQtUHJvY2Vzcw== | U3RhcnQtUHJvY2Vz |
| Start-Process | 1 | X1N0YXJ0LVByb2Nlc3M= / KlN0YXJ0LVByb2Nlc3M= | N0YXJ0LVByb2Nl |
| Start-Process | 2 | X19TdGFydC1Qcm9jZXNz / KipTdGFydC1Qcm9jZXNz | TdGFydC1Qcm9jZXNz |

### Obfuscated Payload with Special Characters

Adversaries may also obfuscate the PowerShell script using special characters.

To detect this, look for:
- Execution of powershell.exe with the -nop, -w hidden, and -c arguments
- High counts of obfuscation characters like `, `, and '

Useful telemetry will include:

- Windows Security Event ID 400: PowerShell command-line logging
- Windows Security Event IDs 800 and 4103: Module loading and Add-Type logging
- Windows Security Event ID 4688 : A new process has been created including process command-line
- Sysmon Event IDs 1 and 7: Process creation and Image loaded

Tuning considerations:
- Monitor for any attempts to enable scripts running on a system would be considered suspicious.
If scripts are not commonly used on a system, but enabled, scripts running out of cycle from patching
or other administrator functions are suspicious. Scripts should be captured from the file system when
possible to determine their actions and intent.
- Monitor for newly executed processes that may abuse PowerShell commands and scripts for execution.
PowerShell is a scripting environment included with Windows that is used by both attackers and administrators.
Execution of PowerShell scripts in most Windows versions is opaque and not typically secured by antivirus
which makes using PowerShell an easy way to circumvent security measures.
- Encoded PowerShell can be abused to avoid any complexity with special characters that can be difficult
to handle.

1243b63d-71f0-4073-8c55-9afc9e0e216f.name: PHP SAPI Worker Spawning a Command Interpreter or Network Client
1243b63d-71f0-4073-8c55-9afc9e0e216f.description:
Alerts when a PHP interpreter or web server worker (php-fpm, php-cgi, php, httpd,
apache2, nginx) is the parent of a shell, scripting interpreter, download client,
or network utility on a Linux host.

This is the execution signal of the PHP2Shell objective. It stays deliberately
CVE-agnostic, and the published root cause strengthens rather than weakens that
choice. Calif generalised its first finding into a reusable pattern (publish or
destroy state, perform fallible work, then commit, where a nonlocal fatal skips the
commit and a surviving consumer trusts false state) and that pattern immediately
produced a second bug, so more siblings are likely. AWS reports the same conclusion
from the other direction: patch-to-exploit time is collapsing, and defenders should
invest in detections that do not depend on a per-CVE signature. Attempt-stage
coverage for these two CVEs specifically lives in signals 4 and 5 of the objective,
not here.

A true positive proves arbitrary code execution under the web service account. It
does not prove which vulnerability delivered it: an application-level command
injection, a vulnerable dependency, or an unrelated interpreter bug produce the
same observable. That is the point. The rule keeps working for the next PHP
interpreter flaw and for hosts on no-fix branches (PHP 5.x, 7.x, 8.0, 8.1) that
will never be patched.

WHY apache2 AND httpd MATTER MORE THAN php-fpm HERE

The SAPI decides which exploitation path works, and the result is the opposite of
the usual assumption. Under mod_php the interpreter is embedded in the Apache
worker and request shutdown runs even after a startup failure, so two of the three
paths give RCE against arbitrary PHP scripts and this rule fires with apache2 or
httpd as the parent, with no php process anywhere in the ancestry. Under PHP-FPM
those same two paths take the worker-exit branch (FPM_EXIT_SOFTWARE) and die before
anything consumes the malformed state, so this rule will not fire for them at all;
only the application-dependent unserializer path produces execution on PHP-FPM.
Treat mod_php hosts as the primary surface for this rule and rely on signal 4 for
PHP-FPM attempt coverage.

What this rule does NOT cover:
  - Memory-only payloads that never spawn a child process. Use the egress signal
    of the objective for those.
  - Web shells dropped but not yet invoked. Use the file-write signal.
  - Attempts that exit the PHP-FPM worker without achieving execution, which is
    how the two startup-stage paths present on PHP-FPM. Use signal 4
    (memory_limit fatals and worker exits).
  - The attacker's request shape. Use signal 5, which needs WAF or proxy body
    inspection that this rule does not require.
  - Hosts with no process-telemetry agent, which is the dominant blind spot on
    shared and managed hosting.

Precision: MEDIUM before tuning, HIGH after. Recall risk: MEDIUM (child binary
list is enumerated, so a statically linked or renamed dropper evades it).

The child binary list and the environment filter block are the two tuning knobs.
Enumerate the legitimate PHP callers for each service: deployment and cache-warm
hooks, ImageMagick and ffmpeg wrappers, mail transport helpers, and composer in a
container entrypoint are the usual benign parents of a PHP-spawned shell.

DEPLOYMENT POSTURE: the quiet tuning window assumed in version 1 no longer exists.
Exploitation was observed from 2026-10-17, four days before disclosure, and is now
broad. Deploy alerting from this STAGING configuration and tune against live
findings rather than holding the rule back until the exclusion list is complete.
Run the retrospective hunt in step 1 of the analysis procedure before anything
else.

procedure.analysis:
0. ONE-TIME RETROSPECTIVE HUNT, before triaging any individual alert. AWS
   observed PHP2Shell exploitation on 2026-10-17, four days before disclosure,
   so an investigation anchored on the disclosure date starts too late. Run
   this rule's logic backwards over the full retention window with a floor of
   2026-10-17 across every web tier host. Coordinated disclosure began
   2026-08-11 and a researcher published a hash of one finding on 2026-08-05,
   so an earlier bound cannot be excluded, but no exploitation has been
   reported before 2026-10-17. Note the practical ceiling: Defender-style
   endpoint retention is often 30 days, whereas Sentinel workspace retention
   is usually 90 days or more, so the achievable lookback differs by source.
1. Confirm the parent is genuinely a web-facing SAPI worker, not the PHP CLI,
   and record which SAPI. An apache2 or httpd parent means mod_php, where two
   paths give RCE against arbitrary scripts under default configuration: treat
   it as the high-probability case. A php-fpm parent means only the
   application-dependent unserializer path applies, so also check whether the
   application reaches session_start, session_decode, unserialize or a wrapper
   such as WordPress's maybe_unserialize. A plain `php` parent may be a cron
   job or a deployment script, which is usually a different and benign story.
2. Read the full child command line. Download clients fetching to /tmp, /dev/shm
   or a web root, base64-decoded payloads piped to a shell, reverse-shell
   invocations of nc or socat, and chmod +x on a freshly written file are all
   confirmation. A bare interpreter with no arguments is more often an
   application wrapper.
3. Pin the host's PHP exposure: record the version serving web requests (not the
   CLI binary) and the SAPI type. Anything from PHP 5.4.0 onward is in scope,
   and a host on PHP 5.x, 7.x, 8.0 or 8.1 has no upstream fix and should be
   treated as compromised-until-proven-otherwise.
4. Correlate against WAF or proxy logs for the same host in the surrounding
   minutes, looking for the two documented request shapes rather than for
   multipart POSTs generally: (a) a multipart body carrying many upload parts
   with filename="" and deeply nested bracket field names such as
   files[a][b][c], often chunked or over HTTP/2 with no meaningful
   Content-Length; (b) a multipart POST carrying a session ID and the
   PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS field with no file part at all. Shape (b)
   without a file part is the specific exploitation form; the field on its own
   also appears in legitimate upload-progress use. Note that ordinary
   combined-format access logs do not contain POST bodies, so absence of
   evidence here is usually a telemetry gap, not a negative finding. Capture
   the source addresses.
5. Check the source addresses against the anonymisation infrastructure AWS
   published: 103.216.220.92 (seen 2026-10-17), 31.223.184.166, 37.19.200.5,
   134.209.159.64, 103.114.163.188, 95.217.98.37 (all 2026-10-21). AWS states
   these are shared anonymisation infrastructure and not exclusive to this
   activity, so investigate observations rather than blocking the addresses,
   and do not treat a non-match as exoneration.
6. Check for the other objective signals on the same host: new or modified PHP
   files under the web root, and first-seen outbound destinations. Either turns
   this from attempted to established access.
7. Check PHP error logs and PHP-FPM pool logs for the preceding window. The
   expected artefact is a fatal error reporting that the allowed memory size
   was exhausted, because the exploit deliberately drives an allocation past
   memory_limit to produce a controlled fatal. Segfaults are not the signature.
   On PHP-FPM, look for clean worker exits rather than crashes. A burst of such
   fatals before the execution event indicates repeated attempts before one
   landed, and gives the earliest timestamp to anchor scoping on.
8. If the activity matches a known deployment or media-processing workflow,
   verify against the change record, then add the specific full process path to
   the environment filter block rather than widening the rule.

searches.purpose: Web shells and other files written under the web root by the PHP runtime
searches.query:
let lookback = 7d;
let target_host = "<Computer>";
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Computer == target_host
| where ProcessName in~ ("sysmon", "sysmonforlinux")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("php-fpm", "php-cgi", "apache2", "httpd", "nginx")
| extend EventId = extract(@'<EventID>(\d+)</EventID>', 1, SyslogMessage)
| where EventId in ("11", "23")  // FileCreate, FileDelete
| extend TargetFilename = extract(@'<Data Name="TargetFilename">([^<]*)</Data>', 1, SyslogMessage),
         Image          = extract(@'<Data Name="Image">([^<]*)</Data>', 1, SyslogMessage)
| where Image matches regex @"(?i)/(php-fpm[0-9.]*|php-cgi[0-9.]*|php[0-9.]*|httpd|apache2|nginx)$"
| where TargetFilename has_any ("/var/www", "/srv/www", "/usr/share/nginx/html", "/home")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Image, TargetFilename, EventId
| order by TimeGenerated asc

searches.purpose: Multipart POST volume and source addresses against the affected host, from the earliest known exploitation date
searches.query:
``` Replace index/sourcetype with the tenant web access log macro. ```
``` Window floor is 2026-10-17, the earliest exploitation AWS observed, ```
``` not the 2026-10-21 disclosure date. ```
index=web sourcetype=access_combined dest_host="<dest>"
    earliest="10/17/2026:00:00:00" latest=now
| search method=POST
| stats count AS requests,
        dc(uri_path) AS distinct_paths,
        values(uri_path) AS paths,
        min(_time) AS firstTime,
        max(_time) AS lastTime
      BY clientip, status
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - requests

searches.purpose: The two documented PHP2Shell request shapes, where WAF or proxy body inspection exists
searches.query:
``` Requires a source that captures or evaluates POST bodies (WAF, reverse ```
``` proxy, mod_security audit log). Combined-format access logs do NOT ```
``` contain multipart bodies and will return nothing here. Replace the ```
``` index and field names with the tenant WAF sourcetype. ```
index=waf dest_host="<dest>" earliest="10/17/2026:00:00:00" latest=now
| search content_type="*multipart/form-data*"
``` Shape A: many empty-filename parts carrying field names nested at least ```
``` two bracket levels deep, delivered with no meaningful declared length. ```
``` Thresholds are starting points: set them on the shape (high part count ```
``` and deep nesting against a small body), not on exact values, because ```
``` the attacker can vary count, depth and encoding freely. ```
| eval empty_filename_parts=mvcount(split(request_body, "filename=\"\""))-1
| rex max_match=0 field=request_body "name=\"(?<nested_fields>[^\"]*\[[^\"]*\[[^\"]*)\""
| eval nested_field_count=mvcount(nested_fields)
| eval lengthless=if(match(coalesce(transfer_encoding,""),"(?i)chunked")
                      OR coalesce(http_version,"")="2", 1, 0)
| eval shape_a=if(empty_filename_parts>=20 AND nested_field_count>=20, 1, 0)
``` Shape B: upload-progress field present with no file part at all. The ```
``` field name is the server's session.upload_progress.name value and only ```
``` defaults to PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS. ```
| eval has_upload_progress=if(match(request_body,"PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS"), 1, 0)
| eval has_file_part=if(match(request_body,"filename=\"[^\"]+\""), 1, 0)
| eval shape_b=if(has_upload_progress=1 AND has_file_part=0, 1, 0)
| where shape_a=1 OR shape_b=1
| stats count AS requests,
        sum(shape_a) AS shape_a_hits,
        sum(shape_b) AS shape_b_hits,
        max(empty_filename_parts) AS max_empty_parts,
        max(nested_field_count) AS max_nested_fields,
        max(lengthless) AS lengthless_delivery,
        min(_time) AS firstTime,
        max(_time) AS lastTime
      BY clientip, uri_path
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort 0 - requests

searches.purpose: memory_limit exhaustion fatals and PHP-FPM worker exits preceding the alert
searches.query:
// The exploit forces a controlled fatal by exceeding memory_limit, so the
// expected artefact is an out-of-memory fatal, not a segfault. On PHP-FPM
// the startup-stage paths present as clean worker exits.
let lookback = 7d;
let target_host = "<Computer>";
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Computer == target_host
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("Allowed memory size", "memory_limit",
                               "exited with code", "exited on signal",
                               "child exited", "FPM_EXIT_SOFTWARE")
| extend FatalKind = case(
      SyslogMessage has "Allowed memory size", "memory_limit exhausted",
      SyslogMessage has_any ("exited with code", "child exited", "FPM_EXIT_SOFTWARE"), "worker exit",
      SyslogMessage has "exited on signal", "worker signal exit",
      "other")
| summarize Events = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            Sample = take_any(SyslogMessage)
         by Computer, ProcessName, FatalKind, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| order by TimeGenerated asc

searches.purpose: Same parent-child pattern across the rest of the web tier, to scope the campaign
searches.query:
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) AS firstTime max(_time) AS lastTime
    FROM datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    WHERE (Processes.parent_process_name="php-fpm*"
        OR Processes.parent_process_name="php-cgi*"
        OR Processes.parent_process_name="apache2"
        OR Processes.parent_process_name="httpd"
        OR Processes.parent_process_name="nginx")
    BY Processes.dest, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort 0 - lastTime

procedure.containment:
Scale containment to what step 2 of the analysis confirmed.

Confirmed execution (download client, decoded payload, reverse shell):
  - Isolate the host at the network layer, or drain it from the load balancer
    if isolation would take the service down. Preserve it for forensics; do not
    reimage before the web root and PHP-FPM logs are captured.
  - Treat every credential readable by the web service account as exposed:
    application configuration secrets, database credentials, cloud instance
    role tokens and API keys. Rotate them. A web host is a pivot into the
    internal network, so review what that account could reach.
  - Hunt the web root for files written since the first event and remove
    confirmed web shells. A shell removed without rotating credentials leaves
    the attacker their next way in.

Still ambiguous:
  - Capture the process tree, the web root diff and the surrounding access log
    window before anything is restarted. A PHP-FPM reload destroys worker state.

Fleet-wide, independent of this alert:
  - Patch. Upgrading is the only complete remediation for both CVEs; AWS and
    Calif both state that no configuration-only workaround fully addresses
    them. Patch supported branches (8.2, 8.3, 8.4, 8.5) and restart PHP-FPM or
    the web server so the new interpreter is actually loaded. Confirm the
    distribution or hosting provider's backported package covers both CVEs; the
    major-version label alone does not tell you. Measure this in hours, not
    days: AWS reports that a multi-day patch SLA now assumes a delay that no
    longer exists.
  - Prioritise mod_php hosts. Two of the three paths give RCE against arbitrary
    PHP scripts there under default configuration, while PHP-FPM is only
    exposed through the application-dependent unserializer path.
  - Partial mitigations, where patching is genuinely blocked. These are
    Calif's, they differ by SAPI, and they do not replace a patch:
      mod_php   -> memory_limit=-1
      PHP-FPM   -> session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and memory_limit=-1
    memory_limit is the common factor because removing the cap removes the
    fatal the exploit depends on. Flag the trade explicitly to the service
    owner before applying: memory_limit=-1 removes PHP's memory cap and raises
    the risk of host memory exhaustion, so it swaps a code-execution risk for
    an availability risk. It also silences objective signal 4 on that host,
    since the fatal that signal watches for can no longer occur. Disabling
    session upload-progress alone closes one path only and does nothing for
    mod_php.
  - At the edge, where patching is blocked: consider blocking multipart file
    uploads after assessing application impact, and apply the AWS WAF
    mitigations described in AWS's companion post for PHP2Shell.
  - Route PHP 5.x, 7.x, 8.0 and 8.1 hosts to migration or isolation. No upstream
    fix is coming for them, and the affected range reaches back to PHP 5.4.0.

0be66eea-4ae4-4544-811b-52651e20d744.description:
Detect base64 encoded PowerShell payload that could be used to launch 
a process or a script.
The detection applies up to 2 levels of encoded payload (a first payload 
containing a PowerShell command with a second base64 payload).  

### Splunk(Sentinel) investigation guidelines ###

The alert notification contains
- host(src_host): the host on which the process was launched.
- src_user: the account used.
- ParentProcessName(parent_process): the process launching the PS with base64 payload.
- NewProcessName(process): PS.
- CommandLine(command_line): the original command line as seen in logs.
- payload_b64_ascii [and payload_b64]: the first level of encoded payload. 
They are always present.
- payload_level2_b64_ascii [and payload_level2_b64] may also be provided 
if the first level was containing another base64 encoded payload.
For Sentinel Alert, you have to decode the base64 string present in command_line field,
using CyberChef or any base64 decoding tool.  

### SENTINEL alerts triage ###
CATCH uses TIDE_LD_005_CSIRC_WL_Win_Base64_Encoded_PS_Payload.csv
to filter legitimate or benign base64 encoded payloads used by PowerShell 
on EC Windows devices running on our Azure IaaS & PaaS tenant.

### ES-SPLUNK alerts triage ###
CATCH uses SOC_LT_289_WIN_reviewed_base64_encoded_payload-exclude.csv
to filter legitimate or benign base64 encoded payloads used by PowerShell 
on EC Windows devices.

05a17237-cf8b-4c14-a8b7-e57886877cf3.name: PHP2Shell - PHP Core Remote Code Execution

threat.description:
Pre-authentication remote code execution in the PHP core interpreter, tracked as
CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and named PHP2Shell by the discovering
researchers at Calif. Each is rated CVSS v4.0 9.2. Patched releases shipped
2026-10-21 after an embargo break forced the date forward. Exploitation is
confirmed, broad, and predates disclosure.

ROOT CAUSE (confirmed by the discoverers, no longer speculative)

The bug class is interrupted cleanup. PHP leaves dangling pointers and stale
interpreter state when an allocation would exceed memory_limit, or when another
fatal error interrupts native code before its normal cleanup completes. Request
shutdown then frees memory that surviving state still references. Calif found
two general OOM fatal producers and three distinct interruptible points. The
earliest affected path dates to PHP 5.4.0, and the paths are exploitable under
default configuration.

HOW THE ATTACKER FORCES THE FATAL

Two request-shaping tricks, both of which leave structural traces a proxy can
see:

  1. post_max_size bypass. PHP compares post_max_size against the declared
     Content-Length before automatic POST parsing, but does not enforce the same
     limit against the bytes it actually consumes. A chunked HTTP/1.1 or a
     lengthless HTTP/2 multipart request therefore passes the check with no
     meaningful declared length. A configured input-decompression filter creates
     the same mismatch between compressed and decoded length.
  2. Memory exhaustion while staying under post_max_size. An RFC1867 upload part
     with filename="" carries no file data and is not counted toward
     max_file_uploads, yet PHP still creates all six $_FILES entries (name,
     full_path, type, tmp_name, error, size). When the field name is nested, for
     example files[a][b][c], PHP builds that hierarchy separately for each of the
     six entries, so one short empty-upload record expands into many native
     HashTables, Buckets and string-key allocations. Hundreds of such records
     exceed the default 128 MiB heap while the whole body stays under the default
     8 MiB post_max_size.

THREE EXPLOITATION PATHS, AND WHY THE SAPI DECIDES EVERYTHING

This is the most operationally important part of the writeup, because it inverts
the usual assumption that PHP-FPM is the main surface.

  Path 1, Apache mod_php, PHP >= 7.3, arbitrary PHP scripts.
    _zend_hash_str_add_or_update_i increments both nNumUsed and nNumOfElements
    before the bucket is initialised, so the bucket becomes teardown-visible
    before its key allocation. A fatal in that allocation skips the key, hash and
    zval assignments while the count stays incremented, and teardown later
    consumes stale bytes as a live bucket. Reached through ordinary request
    variable registration during php_request_startup(), before the target script
    runs.

  Path 2, Apache mod_php, PHP >= 5.4.0, arbitrary PHP scripts.
    Session upload-progress opens and updates a session while the request body is
    still being parsed, before PHP considers its modules activated. If parsing
    fatals, the multipart END callback is skipped and request shutdown gates
    extension shutdown on the activation flag, so session RSHUTDOWN never runs.
    The heap is freed anyway and the Apache worker survives with PS(id) and
    PS(http_session_vars) dangling. A second multipart request carrying a session
    ID and the PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS field but NO file part reaches
    MULTIPART_EVENT_END without passing FILE_START, so the early session reset
    never happens and cleanup operates on freed state.

  Path 3, Apache mod_php and PHP-FPM, application-dependent.
    PHP's generic unserializer publishes shared bookkeeping in the Basic
    extension's globals. A fatal inside a live decode skips
    php_var_unserialize_destroy(), leaving BG(unserialize).data dangling with a
    nonzero nesting level. Because this fatal lands after successful request
    startup, PHP-FPM keeps the worker. The next multipart request reaches session
    upload-progress before Basic's RINIT and the stale nesting level makes the
    dangling pointer look like an active nested decoder. Requires the application
    to expose a reachable post-startup decode: session_start(), session_decode(),
    unserialize(), or a wrapper such as WordPress's maybe_unserialize().

  The asymmetry: on mod_php, PHP runs inside the Apache worker and request
  shutdown executes even after startup failure, so the malformed state is
  consumed and the worker is reused. On PHP-FPM, a startup failure takes the
  process-exit branch (FPM_EXIT_SOFTWARE) and the worker dies before anything
  can consume the state, which is why paths 1 and 2 do not apply to it. mod_php
  is therefore the critical surface: universally exploitable against arbitrary
  scripts. PHP-FPM is exploitable only through path 3 and only where the
  application decodes attacker-influenced or memory-pressure-adjacent data.

CONFIRMED PRE-AUTH RCE TARGETS

Calif confirmed pre-authentication RCE against WordPress 7.1.2, Drupal 11.4.3,
Joomla 6.1.4, MediaWiki 1.46.2, Roundcube 1.7.4, Magento 2.4.9, phpMyAdmin 5.2.3,
Nextcloud 35.0.1, Laravel 13.11, Symfony 8.1 and WHMCS, plus arbitrary PHP
scripts in some instances. This is not a niche configuration issue.

EXPLOITATION IN THE WILD, EARLIER THAN DISCLOSURE

Amazon Threat Intelligence found a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt in MadPot
honeypot telemetry dated 2026-10-17, four days before disclosure, from an IP
associated with a commercial anonymisation network. Further attempts followed
between 02:00 and 08:00 UTC on 2026-10-21, before the 14:00 UTC embargo lift,
with varied payloads and anonymisation infrastructure suggesting multiple
distinct actors. More proof-of-concept code appeared within hours of the release
and was used against AWS sensors almost immediately. It is now broadly exploited.

Investigations should start from 2026-10-17 at the latest, not from the
disclosure date. Coordinated disclosure ran from 2026-08-11 and a researcher
published a hash of one finding on 2026-08-05, so an earlier bound cannot be
excluded, though no exploitation has been reported before 2026-10-17.

LINEAGE: EXPECT SIBLINGS

The class has a twenty-year history. Stefan Esser found the first PHP memory
limit remote vulnerability in 2004; bug #78876 (multipart/form-data causing OOM)
was reported in 2020 and incidentally shielded HHVM; OSTIF and Quarkslab
identified a related issue in a 2024 audit without proving exploitation. Calif
generalised its first finding into a reusable pattern (publish or destroy state,
then perform fallible work, then initialise or commit, where a nonlocal fatal
during the fallible work skips the commit and a surviving consumer trusts false
state) and that pattern immediately produced the second finding. Two consequences
for detection: more siblings are likely in PHP and in comparable interpreters, and
CVE-specific signatures will age badly. Detection content for this threat should
key on the mechanism and on post-exploitation behaviour, not on these two CVE
identifiers.

MITIGATION REALITY

Patching is the only complete remediation. Both AWS and Calif state plainly that
no configuration-only workaround fully addresses both issues. Calif's temporary,
partial mitigations are not what the early reporting suggested, and differ by
SAPI:

  - mod_php: set memory_limit=-1.
  - PHP-FPM: set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and memory_limit=-1.

memory_limit is the common factor, because removing the cap removes the fatal the
exploit depends on. That trade is not free: memory_limit=-1 removes PHP's memory
cap and raises the risk of host memory exhaustion, so it is a deliberate
availability trade, not a safe default. Disabling session upload-progress alone
closes only one path and does nothing for mod_php. AWS additionally suggests
blocking multipart file uploads where patching is blocked, after assessing
application impact, and publishes an AWS WAF mitigation guide.

Content in this description was rephrased from the sources in the references for
compliance with licensing restrictions.
threat.terrain:
Ranked by exploitability, not by population.

Critical: Apache with mod_php on PHP 5.4.0 or later, internet-facing. Paths 1 and
2 give RCE against arbitrary PHP scripts under default configuration, with no
application precondition and no authentication.

High: PHP-FPM and php-cgi behind Apache HTTP or NGINX, where the application
performs a reachable post-startup decode (session_start, session_decode,
unserialize, or wrappers such as WordPress's maybe_unserialize). Path 3 only, so
exploitability is application-dependent, but the qualifying call is present in
most real CMS and framework stacks.

The affected application population covers CMS and e-commerce (WordPress,
WooCommerce, Drupal, Joomla, Magento and Adobe Commerce), collaboration and
webmail (MediaWiki, Nextcloud, Roundcube), administration interfaces
(phpMyAdmin, WHMCS) and framework-based bespoke applications (Laravel, Symfony).

Secondary: CI runners executing PHP build and test code, and container images
pinning a PHP base layer, where a rebuild rather than a package update is needed.
Shared and managed hosting concentrates the unpatchable population and sits
outside direct control.

Inventory note: record the version and SAPI that actually serves web requests.
The CLI binary and the web SAPI can differ on the same host, and the SAPI
determines which of the three paths apply.

bdc58fee-8da6-4fc9-8fbd-30f8fd156bc7.name: Powershell with encoded payload passed to cmdline

threat.terrain:
A threat actors need an initial access to the system to use PowerShell
console to execute commands to obfuscate their traffic and activities.
threat.description:
When working with PowerShell, a threat actor can encode a command or script
using Base64 or other type of encoding and pass it as a parameter to the
command line. This technique is useful for obfuscating sensitive
information or executing complex commands. (ref [1])   


The malicious document contains a macro which, upon execution,
creates a batch script at C:\Users\public\new[.]bat with the
following content:  

powershell -exec bypass -noP -w hidden -nonI -enc"{string}" del %0;

Other possible examples for encoding with PowerShell commands: 

Encoding a Command with Base64

1. Create a command as a string. 

$command = 'dir "C:\Program Files"'

2. Convert the command to Base64:

$bytes = [System.Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetBytes($command)
$encodedCommand = [Convert]::ToBase64String($bytes)

Now you can run the encoded command using powershell.exe:

powershell.exe -encodedCommand $encodedCommand

It's also possible to encode domain names, for example: 

Powershell input:

[Convert]::ToBase64String([System.Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetBytes("'sample_domain.com'"))

Threat actors also use PowerShell scripts for faster encoding process and result.  

An example of Powershell script (ref [2])  

param(
[Parameter()][Alias("un")][string]$Username,
[Parameter()][Alias("pw")][string]$Password
)

Write-Host "Username: $Username"
Write-Host "Password: $Password"

3c0b7355-2f44-4632-89a9-a9cdb4fa9de9.name: PHP2Shell Exploitation and Post-Exploitation on the Web Application Tier

objective.description:
Detect exploitation of the PHP core remote code execution flaws CVE-2026-109618
and CVE-2026-109619 (PHP2Shell) at both the attempt stage and the
post-exploitation stage.

Version 1 of this objective covered post-exploitation only, on the reasoning that
no trigger signature was possible. That reasoning is now obsolete. Calif has
published the root cause, and the mechanism turns out to have structural features
an attacker cannot easily vary: the exploit must first force a PHP fatal by
exceeding memory_limit, and the cheapest way to do that is a multipart body
stuffed with empty-filename upload parts carrying deeply nested bracket field
names, delivered chunked or over HTTP/2 so the declared length never trips
post_max_size. Two of the three paths then require a follow-up multipart request
carrying PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS with no file part. Those are request
properties, not payload bytes, so they survive payload obfuscation.

The objective therefore has two halves. Signals 4 and 5 cover the attempt: a
server-side view (memory_limit fatals and PHP-FPM worker exits) and a
request-side view (multipart shaped for heap exhaustion). Both can fire before
the attacker achieves anything, which matters because AWS observed exploitation
from 2026-10-17, four days before disclosure. Signals 1 to 3 cover what the
attacker does with code execution once they have it, and they are what makes this
objective durable: Calif generalised the bug into a reusable pattern and expects
siblings, so CVE-specific coverage will age while behavioural coverage will not.
AWS reaches the same conclusion independently and advises investing in detections
that do not depend on a per-CVE signature.

SAPI ASYMMETRY DRIVES COVERAGE, AND IT IS COUNTERINTUITIVE

On Apache mod_php, PHP runs inside the Apache worker, request shutdown runs even
after a startup failure, and the worker is reused. Exploitation succeeds against
arbitrary PHP scripts, and the post-exploitation signals fire with apache2 or
httpd as the parent process, never a php binary. On PHP-FPM, a startup failure
exits the worker before anything can consume the malformed state, so two of the
three paths simply do not work, and an attempt shows up as a worker exit rather
than as code execution. The practical consequence: signals 1 to 3 carry mod_php
coverage, signal 4 carries PHP-FPM attempt coverage, and only the
application-dependent third path produces execution on PHP-FPM. A detection
estate that watched only php-fpm process ancestry would have had the asymmetry
exactly backwards.

Scope boundary: this objective covers exploitation and post-exploitation on the
PHP application tier. It does not cover interpreter inventory or version exposure,
which is vulnerability-management work, nor the partial configuration mitigations
(memory_limit=-1 on mod_php, plus session.upload_progress.enabled=0 on PHP-FPM),
neither of which replaces a patch. It also does not include matching on the
anonymisation-network addresses AWS published: AWS states they are shared
infrastructure to investigate on observation rather than block, so they belong in
rule triage procedures, not in a detection.

signals.name: PHP SAPI worker spawns an OS command interpreter or network client
signals.description:
A process whose parent is a PHP interpreter or web server worker (php-fpm,
php-cgi, php, httpd, apache2, nginx) executes a shell, scripting
interpreter, download client, or network utility. This is the highest
fidelity observable for the objective: a healthy PHP application tier
rarely shells out, and when it does the set of legitimate callers is small
and enumerable per environment.

The apache2 and httpd parents are not padding. Under mod_php the
interpreter is embedded in the Apache worker, so successful exploitation of
the two universally exploitable paths produces a child of apache2 or httpd
with no php process anywhere in the ancestry. mod_php is the critical
surface here, which makes those two parent names the most important entries
in the list rather than an afterthought.

True positive proves arbitrary code execution under the web service
account, independent of which vulnerability or application flaw delivered
it. Known benign callers: deployment and cache-warm hooks, ImageMagick and
ffmpeg wrappers, mail transport helpers, and composer running in a
container entrypoint. These are environment-specific and must be enumerated
into the rule exclusion block rather than removed from the signal.

data.availability: Linux endpoint process telemetry on the web application tier
data.requirements:
Process-creation events with both the child image and the parent image.
Sysmon for Linux (event ID 1), Falco, Tetragon, or an EDR agent satisfy
this. Plain auditd EXECVE records do not: they carry a numeric ppid but
no parent image, so the parent must be resolved by correlation, which
degrades precision. Declare the agent coverage gap for any web host that
has none.

signals.name: Web-served file written by the PHP runtime
signals.description:
A PHP SAPI worker, or an Apache worker running mod_php, creates or modifies a
file under a web-served directory, most significantly a single-file PHP
script with obfuscated content. This is the persistence half of the attack: a
web shell in a writable web root survives the interpreter patch and gives the
attacker a stable channel that no longer depends on the vulnerability. It
also survives the mitigation path, since memory_limit=-1 removes the fatal
the exploit needs but does nothing about access already established.

Precision depends entirely on how the application manages its own writable
paths. Upload directories, template and asset caches, and session storage
are legitimately written by PHP all day. The signal is only usable once
those paths are enumerated and excluded, and it is strongest when scoped to
files that the web server will interpret as code.

data.availability: Linux endpoint file telemetry on the web application tier
data.requirements:
File-create and file-modify events with the writing process image and the
target path. Sysmon for Linux (event ID 11), Falco, Tetragon, or EDR
file telemetry satisfy this. Requires a maintained inventory of web-root
paths and application-writable subdirectories per service to be tunable.

signals.name: First-seen egress from a web tier host after an inbound request burst
signals.description:
A host in the web application tier opens an outbound connection to a
destination not seen in its own historical baseline, shortly after a burst
of inbound requests. Covers the command-and-control and tool-transfer step
